Today, we’re committing a portion of Anthropic’s shares to the Anthropic Public Benefit Fund,
a new wholly owned entity with a structure that increases the stake as the company grows. Subject to stockholder approval, 5% of Anthropic’s shares will be committed today, with an additional 2% added at the board’s discretion for every 50% increase in the company’s value above a set baseline.
As a public benefit corporation, most of our work in pursuit of our mission takes place inside the company: research relevant to AI safety and interpretability; applied biomedical research; discounts on Claude for nonprofits and scientific institutions. These activities have both a public benefit component and for-profit value, so we house them directly in the company.
The Anthropic Public Benefit Fund will have increased flexibility and scale, enabling us to pursue our mission in new ways: for example, we might explore large donations to traditional nonprofits or direct distributions to specific populations.
One example is labor market impacts. AI may generate enormous economic value, but it could also cause instability for many workers. Anthropic has already committed
$200 million
to studying and addressing this issue, but given the pace of AI progress, bolder approaches may be needed. The Fund will have the versatility to pursue them.
We’re establishing the Anthropic Public Benefit Fund as an LLC—rather than a 501(c)(3) or other format—to give adjustability between different forms of giving. None of the Anthropic equity held by the LLC will be used for lobbying or political giving, in the US or abroad.
Because of the way the Fund is structured, the more Anthropic grows, the larger the share of the company that can be dedicated expressly to the public good. It is common practice for tech companies to offer escalating compensation awards to their executives. We are instead directing that equity to the public benefit.
This builds on commitments our co-founders and employees have already made. When Anthropic was founded, our co-founders pledged to donate 80% of their equity holdings, and since founding we have also operated an equity donation match program that allows employees to pledge equity which Anthropic matches. Approximately half of our employees participate in this program. When combined with today’s announcement, roughly 20% of Anthropic shares will be dedicated to the public good, plus any additional percentage that could be added if the company reaches specific valuation milestones.
In the coming months, we will share more about the Anthropic Public Benefit Fund’s structure and governance, including the valuation milestones that may add to its stake. We will also report on our progress to date against our mission in an upcoming public benefit report.

Our mission
We build the foundation for understanding AI’s economic impact. The Anthropic Economic Index tracks how AI tools are being used around the world and across every sector of the economy. Alongside regular Economic Index reports, we produce novel research that studies the economic implications of AI, and fund ambitious external research.
Producing reliable data to guide policy
The speed of AI development means the stakes are unusually high. We need reliable data to inform the decisions that workers, employers, and policymakers make about the future. Our research provides evidence to address uncertainty and help society navigate this transition.

Monthly API credits for Max and Team plans
Updated this week
Copy for LLM
Max and Team plans include monthly credits for the Claude Platform. Use them to build Claude into your own apps and agents with the Claude API. This article explains who's eligible, how to claim your credit, what it covers, and what happens when it runs out.
Available on Max and Team plans, including discounted Team plans. Free, Pro, and Enterprise plans aren't eligible.
Monthly credits by plan
Plan
Monthly credit
Max 5x
$100
Max 20x
$200
Team (Standard seats)
$20 per seat*
Team (Premium seats)
$100 per seat*
Discounted Team plans (Nonprofit, Scientists)
$20 USD per Standard seat and $100 USD per Premium seat*
*On Team plans, credits for all seats are pooled into one monthly balance, capped at $500. For example, a team with three Standard seats and two Premium seats receives $260 a month. The pool is calculated from the seats on the plan when the credits are granted.
Eligibility
Active plan.
Your Max or Team subscription must be active and in good standing.
Seven days on the plan.
New subscribers can claim once they've been on an eligible plan for seven days.
Mobile subscriptions.
You can subscribe on the web, iOS, or Android. Claim your credits on claude.ai in a web browser.
No payment method needed.
You don't need to add a card on Claude Platform to claim or use the credit.
How to claim your credit
To claim your credit, you link a Claude Console organization to your plan. Credits go to that organization each month.
Before you begin, you need:
On your Claude plan:
Max: be the subscriber. Team: be a Primary Owner or Owner
In the Console organization:
the Owner, Admin, or Billing role. If you don't have a Console organization yet, you can create one during the claim flow or at
platform.claude.com
.
To claim your credit:
On claude.ai, go to
Settings > Billing
as a Max subscriber or
Organization settings > Billing
as a Team Owner or Primary Owner.
In the
API credits
section, select "Link organization."
Choose the Console organization you want to receive the credits, or create a new one.
Review the
Supplemental Credit Terms
, then Link organization.
Your credits appear in that organization's balance, ready to use.
Important:
You can link only one Console organization, and each Console organization can receive credits from only one plan. You can't change the linked organization yourself, so choose the one you plan to build in. To change it later,
contact support
.
Tip:
Sign in to the Claude Console with the same email you use on claude.ai. If you’re seeing errors during the linking flow, please try again in a few hours.
What the credits cover
The credits work with any available Claude model on the Claude Platform, including:
The Claude API (Messages API and Message Batches API)
The Playground in the Claude Console
Claude Managed Agents
The Claude Agent SDK
The credits don’t apply to:
Interactive Claude Code in the terminal, IDE, desktop, or web
Extra usage in Claude, Claude Code, or Claude Cowork
Claude on Amazon Bedrock, Google Cloud Vertex AI, or Microsoft Foundry
How the credits work
Refreshes each billing cycle.
New credits arrive shortly after your plan payment goes through. On annual plans, credits arrive monthly.
Doesn't roll over.
Unused credits expire at the end of each billing cycle.
Used first.
Your monthly credits are spent before any credits you've purchased.
Shared across the organization.
Everyone with an API key in the linked organization draws from the same balance.
Separate from your plan limits.
The credits don’t change your usage limits in Claude, Claude Code, or Claude Cowork.
Visible in the Console.
All credits appear on the
Billing
page (platform.claude.com/settings/billing) in the Claude Console with their amount and expiry date.
What happens when your credits run out
If the organization has purchased credits or auto-reload,
usage continues and draws from those.
If the organization has no other credits,
API requests stop until your next monthly credits arrive. Usage is never charged to your Claude plan. To keep going, buy credits or turn on auto-reload in the Console.
If your organization is invoiced through Anthropic sales,
usage beyond the credits is billed as usual.
If your plan changes
Cancel, downgrade to an ineligible plan, or refund.
New credits stop. Credits you already have stay usable until they expire.
Upgrade from Max 5x to Max 20x.
You receive prorated credits right away, then $200 each billing cycle after that.
Move from Max to Team.
Your Max link ends. A Team Owner or Primary Owner can claim the team's credits once the Team plan has been active for seven days.
For Team Owners and Primary Owners
One claim for the whole team.
One owner links a Console organization and claims the pooled credit, up to $500 a month.
The pool follows your seat count.
It's calculated from the seats on your plan each time credits are deposited. For example, a team with three Standard seats and two Premium seats receives $260 a month. Adding another Premium seat would increase the next cycle’s credits to $360.
Control who spends it.
Everyone with an API key in the linked organization can use the balance. To limit usage by project or teammate, set
workspace spend limits
in the Console.
Frequently asked questions
Why can't I use the credits for Claude Code?
The credits are for building your own apps and agents on the Claude Platform. They don't cover interactive Claude Code sessions or extra usage after you hit your plan's limits.
Why don't I see the offer yet?
We’re rolling out API credits over a few days so we might not have gotten to you yet. The offer appears after you've been on an eligible plan for seven days. If you're past seven days and still don't see it, check that you're on a Max or Team plan and that you have one of the required roles. If you think you should be eligible but don’t see the API credits,
contact support
.
Is this the same as the Agent SDK credits announced in June?
No. That credit isn't available. API credits cover the Claude API, Claude Managed Agents, and the Claude Agent SDK, and you claim it into a Console organization.
Can I split my credits across multiple organizations?
No. Credits go to a single Console organization.
I'm on a Pro plan. Can I get this credit?
No. The credits are available on Max and Team plans only.
Does this cover
claude -p
?
API credits cover
claude -p
and the Claude Agent SDK when you run them yourself with an API key from your linked Claude Console organization, because that usage is billed as Agent SDK usage. When you're signed in with your Claude plan instead,
claude -p
and Agent SDK usage still draw from your plan's usage limits and don't use your API credits. Runs started by the Claude Code GitHub Action, an IDE extension or the Claude desktop app count as Claude Code usage, so API credits don't cover them, even with
-p
.

AI-Generated Summary
RFD4-Proteina
co-designs protein sequences and all-atom structures using reward-guided inference-time search to focus compute on promising candidates.
The model combines explicit backbone coordinates with latent representation, removing the separate inverse-folding handoff required by prior approaches.
Residue-level latent representation and engineered diffusion reduce sampling from about 400 steps to 60, delivering 3.8x faster generation and 84% less peak memory than
RFD3
at 200 residues.
Both the open model and
NIM microservice
accept annotated CIFs or condition specifications for tasks such as PD-L1 binder design with hotspot constraints.
Inference-time search integrates CUDA-accelerated oracles including
OpenFold3
and
TMol
to score and refine designs against geometry, interaction, and confidence metrics.
rfd4-proteina-campaign
and
rfd4-proteina-package
skills coordinate generation, search, evaluation, and results archiving for iterative design campaigns.
Next Steps
Explore the
RFD4-Proteina NIM microservice
for rapid inference deployment with an HTTP interface.
Explore the
open model on GitHub
for training, inference, method development, and direct control over sampling code.
Point your agent at
BioNeMo Agent Toolkit skills
to coordinate generation, search, and evaluation in automated campaigns.
Powered by NVIDIA Nemotron. AI-generated content may summarize information incompletely. Verify important information.
Learn more
Protein design is a search problem. Choose amino acids for an eight-residue protein sequence and more than 25 billion combinations are possible. Choose amino acids for a 100-residue protein sequence and the number of possibilities exceeds the number of atoms in the observable universe. Somewhere in that space is a protein that opens a path to a new therapy. There are too many combinations to search exhaustively, so finding it depends on knowing where to look.
RFD4-Proteina
, an NVIDIA
BioNeMo
open model co-developed with the Institute for Protein Design at the University of Washington’s School of Medicine, navigates that space using patterns learned from nature. It co-designs protein sequences and all-atom structures, and uses reward-guided inference-time search to focus compute on the most promising candidates.
This tutorial shows computational biologists, ML engineers and drug discovery researchers how to design protein binder candidates against PD-L1, an oncology target, using reward-guided inference-time search and introduces experimental validation results across design tasks.
You can access RFD4-Proteina in two ways:
Choose the
open model
for training, inference, method development, and direct control over sampling code or
Choose the
NIM microservice
for rapid inference deployment with an HTTP interface
Building on
Proteina-Complexa
’s partially latent approach, RFD4-Proteina combines explicit backbone coordinates with latent representation, learned sequence and atomistic variables. Its autoencoder decoder produces the sequence and all-atom structure together, removing the separate inverse-folding handoff to a model such as
ProteinMPNN
.
Prerequisites
Open model
Supported Linux GPU host and Python 3.12; follow
the repository setup guide and use a supported NVIDIA GPU.
Model cache:
Setup downloads the Hugging Face bundle automatically; set HF_HOME only if you want a different cache directory.
NIM
Self-host:
x86_64 or arm64 Linux meeting the
NIM prerequisites
, Docker, NVIDIA Driver, NVIDIA Container Toolkit, and an
NGC API key
.
NIM API endpoint (not recommended for production runs):
HTTP access through NVIDIA
build.nvidia.com
via Shell and Python scripts, no local GPU or model installation required.
About RFD4-Proteina
Figure 1. RFD4-Proteina uses molecular context, design constraints, and design regions to generate protein sequences and all-atom structures, with optional reward-guided search to guide generation
The search loop shown in Figure 1, above, is where RFD4-Proteina focuses its compute.
During inference-time reasoning search, the model denoises generation trajectories to obtain structures, scores these designs, retains and branches promising partial states, and continues until the generation criteria are reached.
Rewards can measure geometry, interactions, or independent prediction confidence. This kind of extra search optimizes designs against a specified objective to yield higher-scoring designs. Later in this tutorial, you will see how a user can enable this functionality through the open model and the NIM.
RFD4-Proteina is faster and uses less memory than RFD3 for several reasons:
It works on a residue-level latent representation instead of atom-level, which avoids memory blow-up.
Engineering of the diffusion process cuts sampling from about 400 steps in Proteina-Complexa to 60, and computation is concentrated on the parts of the process that matter most thanks to reasoning capabilities in the model.
Inference-time search is also faster, since the oracles (OF3 and physics methods like
tmol
) are CUDA-accelerated.
The model and kernels were co-designed with the cuEquivariance and BioNeMo Inference Runtime (BIR) teams for speed and scalability.
Figure 2. At 200 residues, RFD4-Proteina delivers 3.8x faster generation and uses 84% leeds peak reserved memory than
RFD3
in the reported generation benchmark
From a molecular design idea to candidate designs
Figure 3. The reference workflow links molecular design, computational evaluation, and experimental testing in an iterative cycle
The workflow in Figure 3, above, demonstrates how to use RFD4-Proteina to go from a scientific objective to candidates for experimental testing. An
agent
can coordinate these tools and track results, while scientists define the objectives and use experimental evidence to guide the next round.
Preparing the molecular inputs and environment
Begin by defining the criteria and requirements for generation. For example, RFD4-Proteina expects users to define what may change, what must remain fixed, and computational and experimental success criteria.
Use AtomWorks to generate /manipulate the input data.
AtomWorks
is the molecular data layer used to prepare structures and design annotations for RFD4-Proteina. Its Python and PyMOL workflows prepare fixed atoms, designable residues, hotspots, and molecular context. Preserve the supplied ligand or motif chemistry when designing surrounding protein.
Both the open model and NIM accept annotated CIFs or a condition specification plus its source structure. The specification below fixes the target and defines the new binder.
The repository’s cropped PD-L1 structure from
PDB 5O45
serves as the target. Fix the target’s sequence and backbone coordinates, allow its side chains to repack, and direct binder generation toward hotspot atoms on Tyr56, Met115, and Tyr123. The new binder has 100–150 residues, with free sequence and coordinates.
Clone the repository, then run the examples from its root. This writes
pdl1.json
; both paths use the same target CIF and conditions.
git clone https://github.com/RosettaCommons/RFD4-Proteina.git
cd RFD4-Proteina
cat > pdl1.json <<'JSON'
{
"pdl1_binder": {
"input": "docs/examples/inputs/5o45_cropped.cif",
"contig": "100-150, /0, A17-131",
"conditions": {
"C_CRD": {"true": [{"select": "sel('A') and is_protein_backbone"}]},
"C_SEQ": {"true": [{"select": "sel('A')"}]},
"C_HOT": {"true": [
{"select": "sel('A/*/56/[CG,OH]')"},
{"select": "sel('A/*/115/[CG,SD]')"},
{"select": "sel('A/*/123/[CD2,OH]')"}
]}
}
}
}
JSON
Open model setup
On a supported Linux/CUDA system, install the repository environment with a current uv release (validated with 0.12.24). If uv is already installed, update it first so it recognizes CUDA 13.2. Setup caches the Hugging Face model bundle, including the paired autoencoder. While the model repository is private, authenticate with hf auth login using an account with access.
bash setup.sh --native
source .venv/bin/activate
NIM environment setup
To host the NIM, run this block in Bash on a supported GPU host with Docker and NVIDIA Container Toolkit installed.
read -rsp 'NGC API key: ' NGC_API_KEY; echo
export NGC_API_KEY
printf '%s' "$NGC_API_KEY" | docker login nvcr.io \
-u '$oauthtoken' --password-stdin
image=nvcr.io/nim/ipd/rfd4-proteina:latest
docker pull "$image"
export RFD4_NIM_IMAGE="$(docker image inspect \
--format '{{index .RepoDigests 0}}' "$image")"
printf '%s\n' "$RFD4_NIM_IMAGE" > nim-image.txt
export LOCAL_NIM_CACHE="$HOME/.cache/nim"
mkdir -p "$LOCAL_NIM_CACHE"
docker run -d --rm --name rfd4-proteina \
--runtime=nvidia --gpus 'device=0' -p 8000:8000 \
-e NGC_API_KEY -v "$LOCAL_NIM_CACHE":/opt/nim/.cache \
--shm-size=16g "$RFD4_NIM_IMAGE"
Generate sequences and structures
Open-model generation
Save the following as
design.py
in the repository root. The same script supports generation and search.
Proteina.from_pretrained("nvidia/RFD4-Proteina")
loads the current Hugging Face model and paired autoencoder checkpoints.
import hydra
from rfd4_proteina import Proteina
from rfproteina.generate import run_generation
@hydra.main(config_path="configs", config_name="inference", version_base="1.3")
def main(cfg):
model = Proteina.from_pretrained("nvidia/RFD4-Proteina")
run_generation(cfg, model=model)
if __name__ == "__main__":
main()
Generate one candidate from the repository root:
python design.py inputs=pdl1.json out_dir=runs/pdl1-open seed=42 compile_lengths=null
Outputs are saved under runs/pdl1-open/inference_samples/. Add num_replicates=10 for ten candidates and choose a new out_dir for each run. Hugging Face caches downloads; add revision=”<commit>” to from_pretrained to reproduce a particular model version.
NIM generation
Save this as
nim_client.py
. It sends the PD-L1 condition spec and target CIF to the NIM, then saves generated structures and response metrics.
import json
from pathlib import Path
import requests
spec = json.loads(Path("pdl1.json").read_text())["pdl1_binder"]
target = Path(spec["input"])
spec["input"] = target.name
payload = {
"task": "motif_scaffolding",
"input": {"format": "condition_spec", "example_id": "pdl1_binder",
"spec": spec, "files": [{"filename": target.name, "content": target.read_text()}]},
"sampling": {"num_replicates": 1, "seed": 42},
"metrics": {"tags": ["design", "hotspot_conditioning"]},
}
def submit(payload, out):
out.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
response = requests.post("http://localhost:8000/biology/ipd/rfd4-proteina/generative",
json=payload, timeout=1800)
response.raise_for_status()
result = response.json()
(out / "response.json").write_text(json.dumps(result, indent=2))
for i, design in enumerate(result["designs"]):
dest = out / f"design-{i}.cif"
dest.write_text(design["structure"]["content"])
print(design["design_id"], dest)
if __name__ == "__main__":
submit(payload, Path("runs/pdl1-nim"))
Install requests and run the client from the repository root. Keep
pdl1.json
beside the target CIF.
python -m pip install requests
python nim_client.py

Inside NVIDIA Sentry: Secure AI Agents at Runtime
NVIDIA Sentry governs agent access requests, monitors runtime activity, and contains threats from an isolated hardware security layer in milliseconds.
Oct 21, 2026
By
Ofir Arkin
,
Ariel Kit
and
Itay Ozery

AI-Generated Summary
NVIDIA Sentry
monitors AI agents and enforces access policies from a hardware-isolated trust domain on BlueField-4 DPUs, independent of host software.
DOCA Tower acts as a transparent proxy that terminates TLS and evaluates agent requests against Open Policy Agent rules, while DOCA Argus provides real-time memory introspection of the agent's execution environment.
The framework correlates network traffic with runtime context to enforce policies based on container hashes, process integrity, and approved software bills of materials.
Specialized AI models classify agent communications inline or out of band to detect behavioral drift, and in-silicon enforcement can contain agents within milliseconds.
Attested telemetry and tamper-evident records preserved on BlueField-4 support forensic investigation and integration with enterprise security platforms.
Next Steps
Explore
NVIDIA DOCA
libraries and microservices to experiment with out-of-band observability and infrastructure enforcement.
Powered by NVIDIA Nemotron. AI-generated content may summarize information incompletely. Verify important information.
Learn more
An AI agent can complete its assignment and still cross a security boundary. Recent incidents show that agents can circumvent security controls while using tools, credentials, and services to pursue their assigned goals. Monitoring and enforcement need to operate outside the agent’s reach so that it can’t alter or disable them.
NVIDIA Sentry
is a security software framework that monitors AI agents and enforces policies governing their access to models, tools, and data. Part of the
NVIDIA OpenShell reference architecture
announced at GTC Berlin, it’s built on
NVIDIA DOCA
, runs on
NVIDIA BlueField-4 DPUs
, and provides host-isolated runtime protection for AI agents. NVIDIA Sentry validates that an agent operates according to its designed intent and within its defined operational boundaries.
Trusted even when host resources can’t be trusted, it controls the agent’s only path to the model, providing tamper-evident traceability of agent activity while enforcing granular security controls on agent access in silicon. In addition to inspecting agent communications, NVIDIA Sentry uses out-of-band observability to establish real-time situational awareness, continuously evaluating agents’ runtime security and behavior to validate their security and integrity.
This post explains how NVIDIA Sentry evaluates agent requests, detects threats, and enforces security policies independently of host software.
An independent security layer for agent runtime protection
An earlier
agentic AI security
post described how NVIDIA BlueField runs security services in a hardware trust domain independent from the host.
NVIDIA Sentry builds on that foundation to continuously monitor AI agent behavior and enforce access policies independently of host software, establishing a strict security boundary in a separate hardware trust domain outside the agent’s reach to keep agents operating within their designed intent.
Software runtime boundaries remain essential.
NVIDIA OpenShell
is a secure runtime for autonomous agents that governs what an agent can do. OpenShell separates policy enforcement from the agent workload, so a compromised agent can’t change its own restrictions. NVIDIA Sentry adds an independent hardware safeguard out of band, running on BlueField-4, beyond the agent’s reach and knowledge.
In the OpenShell reference architecture, agents execute on
NVIDIA Vera CPUs
, while BlueField-4 sits on the node’s only path to the model. NVIDIA Sentry inspects agent-to-model communications and enforces access policies without relying on the agent to report its own behavior. Memory introspection adds context about the agent’s execution environment, such as a container or microVM, to help detect external threats and agent misbehavior.
Governing agent communications
DOCA Tower is NVIDIA Sentry’s AI security gateway. Built on
Envoy
, the open source edge and service proxy, it operates as a transparent proxy for agent traffic, placing a bidirectional inspection layer between an agent and the external environment.
Agent network traffic reaches BlueField-4 through a direct network I/O path that bypasses host OS/hypervisor packet processing. All of the agent’s network communications are governed by NVIDIA Sentry as BlueField-4 sits on the only path to the model and to the outside world.
An agent’s network access boundary is controlled using DOCA Flow and DOCA Tower, which work in concert to restrict agent access to approved resources. DOCA Flow is used to implement a layer-4 firewall for each agent, accelerated in silicon on BlueField-4. The firewall blocks connections to unauthorized destinations and forwards permitted traffic to DOCA Tower for layer-7 (application layer) inspection, authorization, and additional security checks.
DOCA Tower acts as a transparent proxy, performing Transport Layer Security (TLS) termination using built-in, in-silicon TLS acceleration. For connections configured for inspection, it decrypts the agent traffic permitted by the layer-4 firewall to inspect and control agent communications.
NVIDIA Sentry uses the
Open Policy Agent
(OPA), an open source policy engine, to evaluate access requests against defined policies. OPA uses Rego, a declarative domain-specific language designed to evaluate complex hierarchical data structures. OPA runs locally in memory and can evaluate requests in under a millisecond, depending on policy complexity and configuration.
DOCA Tower is compatible with OpenShell policies, using OPA to extend network access policies and runtime controls into BlueField-4 and to the infrastructure.
Figure 1. NVIDIA Sentry uses DOCA Tower to inspect access requests and a policy engine to evaluate authorization, with runtime context from DOCA Argus
Enforcing agent access policies with runtime context
An agent’s network communications provide only part of the information needed to assess its security and integrity. Visibility into the agent’s execution environment adds context for evaluating access requests that go beyond a traditional resource access policy.
DOCA Argus provides real-time visibility into an agent’s execution environment and operational state, giving NVIDIA Sentry additional context about agent access requests.
It uses live memory introspection to analyze selected regions of volatile host memory and obtain independent evidence of the system’s operational state.
DOCA Argus runs independently of the host, analyzing host memory on BlueField-4 without host-resident agents. This agentless design provides independent runtime visibility while preserving host compute resources. By operating outside the host in its own isolated trust domain, DOCA Argus remains beyond the reach of host software even if the host is compromised.
DOCA Argus maps the execution environment in real time—for example, containers to their respective pods and sandboxes to microVMs—and identifies the running processes and their properties within each environment. It also maps relationships between processes and threads, file access, network connections, loaded libraries, CPUs, GPUs, memory, and other system resources. DOCA Argus tracks containers, processes, and loaded libraries using their associated hashes.
This runtime context enables NVIDIA Sentry to connect agent access requests to the processes and execution environments behind them, enforcing policies that consider both the requested action and the security and integrity of the agent making it.
Using runtime context to evaluate agent access
NVIDIA Sentry correlates network connection information from DOCA Tower with runtime context from DOCA Argus to evaluate access requests. NVIDIA Sentry uses this context to enforce policies based on additional attributes and assertions provided by DOCA Argus. It also enriches tamper-evident records of agent activity with runtime context, reducing the need for downstream correlation.
Figure 1 shows how these checks work. DOCA Tower uses its policy engine to correlate a network connection with the agent’s process that initiated it, its properties, and the container it belongs to. A network access policy can, for example, require that the container’s hash match a list of approved container hashes. It can also require that the initiating process, identified by its hash, appear in the container software bill of materials (SBOM), have permission to initiate network connections, and use an approved execution path and command-line arguments. DOCA Tower then checks whether policy permits the requested access—for example, access to an API and permission to perform the requested action.
NVIDIA Sentry uses DOCA Argus real-time observations and alerts to continuously evaluate agent security. Potential warning signs include executing unapproved tools; using
ptrace
to attack another process or spawn a process that attacks the agent; excessive outbound traffic suggesting data leakage; unauthorized file access or changes; CPU spikes; excessive writes to temporary folders; and large-scale file deletion. When NVIDIA Sentry detects any deviation, it can request millisecond-scale in-silicon containment.
Extending controls to agent interactions
Agent security policies need to govern both what leaves the sandbox and what comes back. Requests can expose sensitive information or initiate unauthorized operations. Responses can introduce malicious instructions or other content that redirects an agent from its assigned goals.
NVIDIA Sentry uses DOCA Tower’s extensible inspection capabilities to apply controls to requests and responses. These controls can:
Apply IP-, URL-, and protocol-level restrictions to agent communications.
Capture tamper-evident records of agent requests, responses, and data flows for behavioral analysis and investigation.
Govern agent-to-agent (A2A) and Model Context Protocol (MCP) traffic.
Detect and redact personally identifiable information and secrets, including API keys, tokens, and passwords.
Identify and block content prohibited by policy.
NVIDIA Sentry evaluates inspected requests and responses throughout an agent’s session, applying policy as the agent accesses models, tools, APIs, and services.
Evaluating agent behavior using specialized models
NVIDIA Sentry integrates with specialized AI models to analyze agent communications and classify agent behavior using tool calls and available reasoning traces. These models run locally or remotely on dedicated GPU-accelerated systems. The classifiers assess whether an agent’s behavior remains consistent with an agent’s designed intent or indicates behavioral drift.
The models can classify agent communications inline or out of band. Inline classification can trigger blocking before potentially harmful content reaches its destination. Out-of-band classification can trigger a response action after detecting agent misbehavior.
Tamper-evident activity records and detection results provide forensic evidence for further incident investigations.
Agent communications require continuous classification to detect misbehavior. DOCA Argus complements this classification with ongoing analysis of the agent’s operational environment to evaluate runtime security and behavior.
Figure 2. NVIDIA Sentry uses DOCA Tower to submit inspected communications to a specialized model for classification, where potentially harmful content is blocked inline
NVIDIA Sentry can contain and quarantine agents within milliseconds using BlueField-4 in-silicon enforcement capabilities without the cooperation of the agent or the host software.
These independent controls matter when software boundaries fail. Even if an agent escapes its sandbox, NVIDIA Sentry retains its monitoring and enforcement capabilities as it operates from BlueField-4’s isolated trust domain.
Enterprise security platforms can also use NVIDIA Sentry telemetry to correlate detections and request response actions. The protected record preserves the observed activity and policy context that led to enforcement for subsequent review.
Figure 3. NVIDIA Sentry combines interaction telemetry, runtime detections, and policy context with enterprise security integrations to drive response actions through DOCA Tower
Using agent identity in access decisions
Security controls must connect an agent’s identity with its permissions and requested action. NVIDIA Sentry uses this identity context in application-layer policy evaluation. DOCA Tower integrates with
SPIFFE/SPIRE
to support verifiable workload identity and supports integration with partner identity systems.
Identity establishes who is making a request. Authorization policies determine which resources an identity may access and which operations are permitted. Runtime evidence adds context about the execution environment associated with the request.
This approach connects identity and runtime security. If an agent’s behavior or integrity changes, NVIDIA Sentry can use that context when evaluating subsequent access requests, applying the organization’s defined policies.
Preserving a trusted record of agent activity
Security teams need evidence for incident investigations, even when an agent has escaped its sandbox or altered host-based logs.
NVIDIA Sentry produces attested telemetry and tamper-evident records using BlueField-4’s independent trust domain. DOCA Tower records inspected communications and policy decisions outside the reach of the agent and host software, while DOCA Argus contributes independently observed runtime signals.
An agent that changes a log inside its own environment cannot make the same change to the protected record maintained on BlueField-4.
Attestation provides verifiable evidence of telemetry’s source and integrity. Security teams can use these records to reconstruct observed interactions, review enforcement decisions, and support audits.
NVIDIA Sentry can supply this telemetry to enterprise security platforms, such as XDR and SIEM platforms and security data lakes, connecting agent activity with broader threat intelligence, detection logic, and incident-response workflows.
Extending NVIDIA Sentry with enterprise security capabilities
NVIDIA Sentry enables developers and cybersecurity providers to extend monitoring, governance, and enforcement through DOCA libraries and microservices.
DOCA Tower uses Envoy’s extensibility, enabling partners to adapt existing plugins or develop new ones to run on BlueField. This provides a familiar foundation for integrating access controls, content inspection, telemetry, and specialized detection logic into the application-layer path.
NVIDIA plans to publish core plugins to accelerate development, including a plugin that exposes agent communications for further analysis of available reasoning traces.
Partners can combine these capabilities with their identity services, AI classifiers, threat intelligence, and security operations platforms. NVIDIA Sentry contributes independent runtime visibility and infrastructure enforcement, while connected platforms add enterprise context and coordinate investigation and response.
Building layered protection for AI agents
Scaling agentic AI requires continuous visibility into and control over what agents can access and do throughout execution. NVIDIA Sentry brings that control into an independent infrastructure domain, combining application-layer inspection through DOCA Tower with runtime evidence and visibility from DOCA Argus and in-silicon enforcement on BlueField-4.
Alongside NVIDIA OpenShell, NVIDIA Sentry extends protection from software execution boundaries to a hardware-isolated safeguard. It enables security teams to evaluate agent identity, authority, interactions, and runtime integrity together—and act when behavior crosses defined boundaries.
Developers and cybersecurity teams can begin exploring these foundations with
NVIDIA DOCA
. Available libraries and microservices, including DOCA Argus, DOCA Flow, and OVS-DOCA, provide a starting point for experimenting with out-of-band observability and infrastructure enforcement ahead of NVIDIA Sentry’s planned availability early next year.

items.title: Powering the Agent Development Lifecycle with any framework, from ADK to LangChain and beyond The Agents CLI Extension System enables developers to use frameworks like LangChain, L
items.content:
Powering the Agent Development Lifecycle with any framework, from ADK to LangChain and beyond
- Google Developers Blog
Powering the Agent Development Lifecycle with any framework, from ADK to LangChain and beyond
OCT. 21, 2026
Pier Paolo Ippolito
Product Manager
Elia Secchi
Solutions Specialist
Share
Facebook
Twitter
LinkedIn
Mail
End to end walkthrough of the new Agents CLI Extension System, with a worked LangChain example and a custom deploy policy
Introduction
When we launched
Agents CLI
at Google Cloud Next '26, we built it around one strong opinion: going from an idea to a production agent on Google Cloud should take a single unified command surface. For teams building with Agent Development Kit (ADK), that opinionated path has worked. You run
agents-cli create
, write the agent logic, and ship to Cloud Run with observability and evals wired up, in about thirty minutes.
The agent framework landscape has grown more diverse in the months since. In addition to ADK, developers today pick between
LangChain
and
LangGraph
, specialized newcomers like
Deep Agents
, or in-house frameworks tailored to a specific business domain. Different teams prefer different frameworks, and the right choice for a greenfield prototype is rarely the right choice for a production migration. Enterprise admins may also have governance policies they want to enforce across the ADLC for all of their development teams, such as: a compliance scan, an SSO gate, a Model Risk Management hop.
Can a team benefit from the deployment, evaluation, and observability work in Agents CLI without being forced to adopt ADK, or without being forced to accept the default behavior of every command? Starting with version 1.5.0, the answer is yes.
Agents CLI now ships with an
Extension System
that lets developers override or add commands without forking the tool.
Version 1.8.0 ships the first-party LangChain extension, which replaces the framework-coupled commands with their LangChain equivalents and leaves the rest of the lifecycle untouched.
We will walk through two journeys below. First, to show you the ADLC with LangChain agents, we'll show you how you can scaffold, run, deploy, and evaluate a LangChain agent through the Agents CLI lifecycle using the first-party extension. Then we build our own small extension that wraps the
deploy
command with a Software Bill of Materials (SBOM) scan, demonstrating the pattern enterprise platform teams can use to enforce their own policies across every project. Both journeys use the same mechanism.
The Framework Lock-in Problem
Most agent development toolchains available today share a limitation: they are opinionated about one specific framework, and the surrounding capabilities (deployment targets, CI/CD pipelines, evaluation harnesses, observability wiring) assume the developer has adopted that framework. When your framework matches the tool's assumption, the opinionated path works. When it does not, you're left with three bad options.
The first is to fork the CLI, maintaining a divergent copy and re-syncing it on every upstream release. You pay a permanent maintenance tax, and every upstream improvement has to be hand-merged into the fork. The second is to wrap the CLI behind custom scripts, building a parallel command surface that invokes the underlying tool. The problem is that developers (and their coding assistants) forget about the wrapper and call the underlying tool directly, bypassing the intended abstraction. The third is to walk away and build everything from scratch, which can consume several engineer-months of work that the team had not planned for, and which rarely produces tooling as polished as the upstream project.
The problem shows up in two scenarios. One is enterprise customers adopting Agents CLI: in regulated industries, a central platform team often requires that every
deploy
invocation be wrapped with a compliance check, that
login
route through corporate single sign-on, or that evaluations flow through a Model Risk Management pipeline. Each of these requirements, implemented today, means either forking the CLI or building a wrapper layer. The other is teams that use ADK most of the time but need to run a non-ADK framework on a specific project. Within the Agents CLI command surface, six commands assume the ADK runtime:
playground
,
run
, and four
eval
subcommands. The other eighteen or so (
scaffold
,
infra
,
deploy
,
publish
,
login
, and friends) are framework-agnostic. Without extensions, choosing a non-ADK framework for a single project meant losing access to all twenty-four.
The Extension System handles both with one mechanism.
What are Agents CLI Extensions?
An Agents CLI extension is a directory in a Git repository that contains a single file called
agents-cli-extension.yaml
. The file declares which built-in commands the extension overrides and which new commands it adds. From the
official documentation
:
Extensions are how you adapt agents-cli to a workflow it doesn't ship with — a different agent framework, an org's deploy policy, or a command of your own — without forking the tool.
Extensions take two shapes, described in the
Using Extensions
page. A command override replaces the behavior of a built-in like
playground
,
deploy
, or
eval generate
. The overridden command receives the user's arguments verbatim, so the user experience stays consistent with the native command. A new command exposes a workflow the CLI does not currently provide as
agents-cli <your-command>
. Both shapes can coexist in the same extension, and most non-trivial extensions use a combination of the two.
Extensions are distributed through Git repositories rather than through a dedicated package registry. The design draws from the extension model used by the
gemini-cli
project. There is no central index to publish to, no package format to maintain, and no ownership roster to apply for. Any directory inside any Git repository can serve as an extension, and Git handles the versioning, pinning, and distribution. For enterprise platform teams, this means creating an internal
platform-extensions
repository and pointing their developers at it, with no external registry to coordinate with.
Reference Forms
An extension can be referenced in several ways, depending on where it lives and how the developer wants to use it:
# First-party shorthand, which resolves to the google/agents-cli repository
agents-cli extension add <name>
# Any organization or repository on GitHub, including self-hosted Git servers
agents-cli extension add acme/platform-extensions
agents-cli extension add acme/platform-extensions#soc2-deploy
# A local path, which is typically used during extension development
agents-cli extension add local@../my-extension
Plain text
Copied
The
#<name>
syntax lets a single Git repository hold multiple extensions, with the fragment identifier selecting one of them. Enterprise platform repositories often bundle together a family of related extensions (one for
deploy
, one for
login
, one for
scaffold create
) under a single repo with shared ownership and release cadence.
Scopes
Extensions install at two scopes. The default is the project scope, where the extension and its lockfile entry are committed to the project's own repository. Teammates and CI pipelines pick it up on checkout. The alternative is the user scope, enabled via the
--global flag
, where the extension is stored in the user's home configuration directory and applies to every project on the machine. The user scope is the one you reach for when an extension needs to be available before any project exists, such as a framework bootstrap extension that configures
agents-cli create
itself.
When both scopes define the same command, the project scope wins, and
agents-cli info
surfaces the source of each active command. Scoping is deliberately explicit: the Extension System will not silently merge or override extensions, and any conflict surfaces to the developer at install time or in the
extension list
output.
Lockfile and Lifecycle
The Extension System follows the discipline of package managers like
uv
or
npm
: it resolves a Git reference to an exact commit SHA at install time, records the resolved SHA in a lockfile, and uses the lockfile to re-materialize the exact reviewed code on every fresh checkout. The
agents-cli install
command restores the vendored working copy from the pinned SHA without advancing the pin, which guarantees that CI and local development run bit-for-bit identical code. To advance a pin to the latest commit on the tracked reference, the developer runs
agents-cli extension update
, which re-resolves the reference and re-prompts for third-party trust. The complete lifecycle is in the
Using Extensions → Lifecycle
section.
The Extension System is marked experimental in v1.8.0. The manifest schema and the command surface may still change in breaking ways before the system is finalized, so teams depending on it should pin their Agents CLI version.
Running LangChain Through Agents CLI
The LangChain first-party extension is a project template: one command scaffolds a working LangChain agent wired into the Agents CLI lifecycle. The resulting project has zero
google-adk
dependency and deploys to Cloud Run through the same code path an ADK project uses. The template's own description reads:
Run LangChain agents, LangGraph graphs, and Deep Agents through the agents-cli lifecycle.
In modern LangChain (version 1.0 and later), the state management layer is provided by LangGraph, so the three frameworks share a common graph representation. The template serves all three communities with the same code.
Prerequisites
Before we begin, we need:
Python 3.11 or later
uv package manager
Google Cloud SDK (gcloud)
Python
Copied
A Google Cloud project with billing enabled is also required. If you do not have one yet, it can be created at
console.cloud.google.com
.
If Agents CLI is not already installed on the development machine, it can be installed in a single command:
uvx google-agents-cli setup
Python
Copied
Finally, we authenticate with Google Cloud and enable the APIs the agent will depend on at runtime:
gcloud auth application-default login
gcloud config set project YOUR_PROJECT_ID
gcloud services enable aiplatform.googleapis.com run.googleapis.com artifactregistry.googleapis.com
Plain text
Copied
Step 1: Scaffolding the Project
Scaffolding and extension installation are the same operation. Rather than installing an extension first and then scaffolding a project, we point
agents-cli create
directly at the extension's template, pinned to a specific release tag:
agents-cli create my-agent \
--agent google/agents-cli/extensions/langchain/template@v1.8.0 \
-d cloud_run
cd my-agent && agents-cli install
Plain text
Copied
The output confirms the scaffold succeeded:
Agents CLI v1.8.0
Fetching remote template: google/agents-cli/extensions/langchain/template@v1.8.0
> Verifying GCP credentials...
> ✓ Connected to project: your-project
✅ Success! Your agent project is ready.
Plain text
Copied
The scaffolded project already contains an
agents-cli-extension.yaml
at its root, which is auto-loaded at project scope the next time any command is invoked. There is nothing to install manually, because the project itself is the extension's installation. A developer scaffolding a LangChain project does not need to know the Extension System exists. The command looks and feels like a native
agents-cli create
invocation that happens to produce a LangChain project instead of an ADK one.
Step 2: Inspecting the Generated Structure
Here's what the scaffolder produced:
my-agent/
├── agents-cli-extension.yaml      # auto-loaded project-scope overrides
├── agents-cli-manifest.yaml       # project configuration (deployment target, etc.)
├── GEMINI.md                      # project's coding-agent guide
├── langgraph.json                 # LangGraph dev-server configuration
├── pyproject.toml                 # langchain, langgraph, langchain-google-genai
├── Dockerfile                     # identical CMD to any ADK project
├── app/
│   ├── agent.py                   # exports root_agent: CompiledStateGraph
│   ├── fast_api_app.py            # exposes `app: FastAPI` on A2A
│   └── app_utils/
│       ├── a2a.py                 # LangGraphAgentExecutor and A2A routes
│       └── telemetry.py           # Cloud Trace and GenAI logging
├── scripts/
│   ├── run.py                     # drop-in replacement for `agents-cli run`
│   ├── eval_generate.py           # drop-in replacement for `agents-cli eval generate`
│   └── publish.py                 # Agent-Runtime-aware refusal wrapper
├── tests/
│   └── eval/datasets/basic-dataset.json
├── deployment/                    # Terraform infrastructure modules
├── uv.lock
└── .agents/skills/agents-cli-langchain/   # the project's own coding-agent skill
Plain text
Copied
The structure looks similar to an ADK project: same
app/
, same
tests/
, same Terraform under
deployment/
, same manifest at the root. The two differences are the
agents-cli-extension.yaml
at the top (which carries the LangChain overrides) and the
langgraph.json
file (which configures the LangGraph dev server used by the local playground).
The main agent definition lives in
app/agent.py
:
"""LangChain agent: a Gemini ReAct agent with a sample tool."""
import os
from dotenv import load_dotenv
from langchain.agents import create_agent

items.title: Announcing New vLLM and SGLang Inference Engines on TPU This post announces native PyTorch backends for vLLM and SGLang powered by TorchTPU, enabling developers to run and optimize
items.content:
Announcing New vLLM and SGLang Inference Engines on TPU
- Google Developers Blog
Announcing New vLLM and SGLang Inference Engines on TPU
OCT. 20, 2026
Qi Zhou
Principal Software Engineer
Chris Chan
Group Product Manager
Share
Facebook
Twitter
LinkedIn
Mail
As part of our
broader announcements
for PyTorch today, we are excited to launch native PyTorch backends for vLLM (developed in partnership with Inferact) and SGLang (developed in partnership with RadixArk).
Background
For years, TPUs have powered large-scale AI workloads with high performance and efficiency. With the rise of agentic and multimodal workloads, serving efficiently is more important than ever. vLLM and SGLang already run on TPU through JAX-based backend, but we kept hearing from developers that they wanted to customize and debug their serving stack in PyTorch.
So we started in earnest on
TorchTPU
, which runs PyTorch natively on TPU. We then built new
vLLM
and
SGLang
engines on top of it.
Our goal is for the PyTorch community to bring models to TPU and make them fast using the tools developers are already familiar with. The engines come with optimized, production-ready serving features and custom Pallas kernels.
The Inference Stack
Serving at scale requires co-design across every layer of the technology stack, from silicon to compilers to orchestration. Today's launch of new inference engines is at the central part of an integrated, open TPU ecosystem.
Engine Overview
TorchTPU makes the TPU a native PyTorch device. Tensors are managed as standard PyTorch tensors on a
tpu
device with no wrapper types, code runs eagerly or compiles via
torch.compile
using XLA, and collectives go through
torch.distributed
.
Because each device runs its own PyTorch process, both engines keep each framework’s worker model, scheduler, KV cache manager and API server etc, and add TPU implementations underneath.
Most models use the standard upstream PyTorch model definitions in vLLM or SGLang, with TPU-specific optimizations in kernels and layer implementations. Custom kernels written in Pallas are called directly from PyTorch as custom operators inside the compiled graph. This platform-plugin design reuses as much of each framework as possible while letting TPU optimizations move at their own pace
Workload support
Both engines are built for the full range of production workloads.
Here’s the list of supported features:
Agentic & Multi-Turn:
Automatic prefix caching, including for hybrid models; KV cache offloading to host memory and Managed Lustre through TPU Sync; tool calling and structured output
Interactive & Low Latency:
Speculative decoding with MTP, EAGLE-3, DFlash, DSpark and n-gram drafters
High-throughput Batch:
Data-parallel attention with expert parallelism
Long Context:
Context parallelism for prefill and decode; FP8 KV cache; host KV offloading
Disaggregated Serving:
Prefill and decode on separate hosts over TPU Sync, including between different parallel layouts
Multimodal:
Vision-language models with image and video input; embedding models
Very Large Models:
Hybrid and sparse-attention architectures, tensor, data, expert, pipeline and context parallelism across hosts; FP8, FP4 (MXFP4, NVFP4), INT8 and INT4 checkpoints
Agentic workloads in particular demand several of these features simultaneously. Because agents repeatedly resend expanding multi-turn conversations, serving them efficiently requires finding the cached prefix instead of recomputing it. Both engines keep reusable prefixes in HBM and, with host offload turned on, automatically move older prefixes to host memory as a second tier.
Moving the KV Cache with TPU Sync
Two of these features move the KV cache away from the device that computed it. Disaggregated serving runs prefill and decode on separate TPU hosts, so each request's KV cache has to travel from the prefill host to the decode host.Tiered KV offload moves the part of the KV cache that no longer fits in HBM to the host's DRAM and secondary storage with Google Cloud Managed Lustre, and brings it back when a later request reuses the prefix. Either way, the transfer has to overlap computation or it adds directly to latency.
Both engines use
TPU Sync
for this. It is an open-source C++ library for KV cache transfer and management on TPU. It reads the device buffers behind PyTorch tensors directly, so a transfer needs no extra staging copy on the host, and it runs transfers on its own threads outside Python while prefill and decode continue. vLLM-TorchTPU exposes it through vLLM's KV connector interface. SGLang-TorchTPU uses it as a disaggregation transfer backend and as the I/O backend for HiCache.
Running today in production & public benchmarks
Both engines are already running at scale in production with preview customers. To provide transparent, reproducible proof of our performance, we benchmark in public through the community-standard SemiAnalysis InferenceX project.
Building on our
initial submission
of Qwen 3.5 on Ironwood TPU (TPU 7x), our engineering teams have further optimized the stack, bringing the lowest cost per million tokens overall to an industry leading
2.01 cents
. Alongside these improvements, we have also published new
state-of-the-art (SOTA) performance results to AgentX
, the project's dedicated track for evaluating agentic long-context and multi-turn workloads. Ironwood TPU leads across most of the Pareto frontier. We look forward to continuously updating our public performance profiles as we bring more models and configurations to the leaderboard.
Building with the community
We did not build these backends in a vacuum. By embracing PyTorch and working directly with open-source project maintainers, we ensure these engines remain upstream-aligned and community-first:
SGLang-TorchTPU was
co-developed
with RadixArk (founded by the creators of SGLang)
This partnership is bringing SGLang's stellar team to build for TPU, delivering an engine that is already running in production at Meta and battle-tested at scale across demanding real-world scenarios.
"SGLang-TorchTPU is running in production at Meta today, and getting there was a close three-way collaboration between Meta, Google, and the SGLang team to make the stack production-ready. It gives us a remarkably mature, PyTorch-native serving stack that integrates effortlessly into our existing AI infrastructure, with the performance, reliability, and flexibility we need to run frontier workloads efficiently on TPUs. " said Zongwei Zhou, PyTorch-TPU lead at Meta.
"At RadixArk, TorchTPU has supercharged our development velocity as we roll out SGLang support across diverse silicon. It’s given us a painless path to native TPU acceleration, passing massive efficiency gains and flexible compute choices directly down to our customers," said Banghua Zhu, CTO and co-founder of RadixArk.
vLLM-TorchTPU was
co-developed
with Inferact (founded by the creators of vLLM)
Together, we integrated a high-performance Pallas
megakernel
for the 2.8T-parameter Kimi K3 model that runs the entire decode step as one kernel, serving more than 700 tokens per second to a single user on Ironwood TPU. Building on this work, Inferact recently led our first preliminary
AgentX submission
for Kimi K3 on the vLLM-TorchTPU stack. This initial milestone already demonstrates exceptional performance per TCO in ultra-high-interactivity workloads, and the rapid increase in the maturity of the vLLM and PyTorch ecosystem on TPU for doing new frontier OSS models bring-up, with follow-up submissions set to unlock even greater efficiency through larger scale prefill/decode disaggregation.
"Our mission at Inferact has always been to make high-performance inference accessible, reliable, and cost-effective across the entire AI ecosystem. We are thrilled to partner on the launch of TorchTPU and bring first-class support for vLLM to TPUs. By bridging PyTorch’s optimized TPU capabilities directly into vLLM, developers can immediately run production workloads on TPUs with the high throughput, low latency, and memory efficiency they expect from our stack," said Simon Mo, CEO and co-founder of Inferact.
To foster continuous open-source contribution, vLLM is also launching a first-of-its-kind community contribution TPU capacity pool to provide free TPU compute to developers who actively contribute to both engines. Request
here
.
Roadmap
As the models get larger, we are evolving both engines to make large-scale TPU inference deployments performant and efficient. The major features for production-grade agentic workloads are already supported. More performance optimizations and advanced features are under way – open a Github issue to request collaboration on yours!
Across the two engines, most of the popular open model families are supported, including Qwen, DeepSeek, GLM, Kimi, GPT-OSS, Gemma4 and more. The team is investing in making more models available to run natively on TPUs, including Day 0 support for new open models. We also want to give the community the tools and TPU capacity to tune performance for their own workloads and configurations.
A note on our JAX runtimes
vLLM-Jax
, and
SGLang-JAX
remain important projects. Both will continue to be maintained, supported, and available for the community to use and adapt.
Getting started
Get started today:
vLLM-TorchTPU:
https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm-torchtpu
SGLang-TorchTPU:
https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang-torchtpu

https://github.com/google-pytorch/torch_tpu

items.title: Unifying Edge AI: How Coral NPU’s open standard brings portable, energy-viable intelligence from model to silicon Google Research has completed the 32-bit open-source Coral NPU RIS
items.content:
Unifying Edge AI: How Coral NPU’s open standard brings portable, energy-viable intelligence from model to silicon
- Google Developers Blog
Unifying Edge AI: How Coral NPU’s open standard brings portable, energy-viable intelligence from model to silicon
OCT. 20, 2026
Billy Rutledge
Eng Director
Google Research
Share
Facebook
Twitter
LinkedIn
Mail
Some of the most compelling use cases for AI are happening directly on the devices around us. You see it first in personal devices like wearables that need to understand context in real time, and increasingly in enterprise and industrial systems like autonomous robots and smart sensors. These experiences require low latency, strict privacy, and all-day reliability that cannot depend on a constant round-trip to the cloud.
Edge AI complements the cloud to bring the best AI experiences. These rely on a continuous flow of context and intelligence across both, working as a model cascade where information is captured and processed in the right place at the right time. Ultra-low-power models on the edge can continuously sense and respond in real time, while seamlessly handing off to larger on-device or cloud models when deeper reasoning is needed.
Still, building for the edge is much harder than it should be. While cloud infrastructure has converged around a few standard software stacks, the edge is split across hundreds of proprietary chip architectures and incompatible toolchains. For ML developers, this creates a heavy fragmentation tax, where you end up rewriting kernels, re-quantizing models, and debugging vendor-specific compilers for every chip you target.
Last year, Google Research
introduced Coral NPU
with a simple idea: an open hardware and software standard is the only way to unify the edge and unlock developer productivity and portability. Our standards based, ML-first RISC-V architecture paired with a reliable open-source toolchain gives developers confidence that their models will compile and run, letting teams optimize a model once and deploy it across different SoC vendors, devices, and power envelopes.
Today, we are reaching three major milestones in the Coral effort:
The complete 32-bit Coral NPU architecture (Milestones 1–4):
Including our
new Matrix Execution Unit
, configurable for up to 1 TOPS and targeting 10mW average power for inference.
The Coral Compiler v1.0, based on IREE/MLIR:
An
open-source, end-to-end compiler
and simulation stack that takes JAX, PyTorch, and TensorFlow models straight to the Coral NPU hardware target.
New MCU chip with Coral NPU:
Unveiling the
2nd-gen Synaptics Astra® SR200 series
(400 GOPS) microcontroller chips.
New Coralboard kits:
Launching
the new Coralboard™ SR
, plus global availability of the Coralboard SL (1 TOPS) from
DigiKey
.
Co-designing silicon and software: The right performance at the right power envelope
Fixing fragmentation at the edge takes more than publishing an instruction set. Historically, many edge accelerators were designed to hit high peak-compute numbers on spec sheets, leaving compiler teams to figure out software support later. In practice, unsupported neural network layers fall back to a general-purpose CPU, which can hurt latency and drain the battery.
We designed the Coral NPU architecture and its compiler together from the start. Instead of chasing peak metrics, our focus is on energy-viable compute: helping to deliver the right performance at the right power envelope for your application.
Completing the Coral NPU 32-bit architecture
Over the past year,
we released the first three milestones
of the 32-bit Coral NPU design: a C-programmable RISC-V scalar frontend for control flow (Milestone 1), an RVV v1.0 vector co-processor for SIMD operations (Milestone 2), and a tightly coupled memory subsystem with floating point support (Milestone 3). With this month's release of the Matrix Execution Unit (Milestone 4), the 32-bit architecture is complete.
Scalar and vector units are great for general control logic and signal processing, but modern ML workloads—from vision encoders to transformer attention layers—spend most of their time on 2D matrix-matrix (GEMM) and matrix-vector (GEMV) multiplication. Running 2D matrix math on a 1D vector engine forces the chip to repeatedly load weights and activations from memory, which can mean spending more energy moving data than doing math.
Our Matrix Execution Unit leverages the RISC-V VME specification (formally part of the Zvt family) to address this need and uses a dedicated outer-product multiply-accumulate (MAC) engine. Because an outer-product engine computes a full 2D tile of operations in a single cycle (256 MACs per cycle), it reuses weights and activations directly inside local registers. This brings quadratic throughput scaling to the core, configurable for up to 1 TOPS.
Having a dedicated matrix engine in a sub-10 mW envelope changes what developers can build on a small battery. Rather than stopping at simple keyword spotting or basic motion detection, devices can run continuous, multimodal workloads, including compact transformer models like Gemma, real-time voice translation on wearables, spatial audio filtering on hearables, and low-latency visual perception on robots.
To help silicon teams bring this open design straight into commercial production, the complete
32-bit RTL
is available today on GitHub.
Bridging models to silicon with the v1.0 IREE/MLIR compiler
To make the hardware easy to target without writing custom assembly, we are also releasing the v1.0 foundation of our
open-source MLIR/IREE compiler toolchain
.
With this stack, you can bring models from JAX, PyTorch, or TensorFlow through standard representations like StableHLO and TOSA. The compiler partitions workloads between the host CPU and the Coral NPU core, handles operator fusion, tiles matrices to fit local SRAM and matrix accumulators, and progressively lowers workloads directly to Coral NPU scalar, RVV v1.0 vector, and VME matrix instructions. Alongside our open-source MPACT simulator and reference FPGA design, hardware and software teams can benchmark models and tune silicon configurations before a chip ever goes to fabrication.
The ecosystem in action: From foundry and IP readiness to commercial silicon
Turning an open standard into commercial silicon takes collaboration across the entire semiconductor value chain. To help silicon partners bring this open design straight into commercial production, the complete 32-bit RTL is available today on GitHub, and we are partnering with
VeriSilicon
on the design implementation and verification (DV) to ensure turnkey readiness for silicon tape-outs. We are also working with
GlobalFoundries
on their 12LP+ FinFET process - accelerating core timing by 70%, and reducing standard-cell area by up to 15% across RTL iterations, with ongoing evaluation of 12LP+ ultra low-power libraries for the Matrix Execution Unit.
On the commercial silicon side, our collaboration with Synaptics shows how quickly this open standard translates into real hardware across very different power budgets without splitting the software experience.
At Synaptics Tech Day (October 20, 2026), Synaptics is launching three
commercial silicon
and
hardware products
built on Coral NPU technology and supported by the open IREE/MLIR toolchain:
2nd-Gen Silicon — Synaptics Astra SR200 Series
: Taped out and launching this month, the
SR200
series integrates second-generation Coral NPU IP (including Milestone 2 RISC-V Vector Core support) to deliver 400 GOPS in an ultra-low-power MCU package. It is built for battery-powered wearables and industrial sensor nodes.
New Synaptics Coralboard SR Unveiled:
A new
Coralboard SR
developer kit powered by the Astra SR200 series, designed for rapid prototyping of MCU-class Edge and Physical AI applications.
Synaptics Coralboard SL Reaches General Availability (GA):
Following our limited-edition preview at Google I/O, the
Coralboard SL
is now generally available worldwide through
DigiKey
, with SDKs and documentation on the
Synaptics Coralboard Developer page
. Powered by the Astra SL2619 processor with a 1 TOPS Torq™ / Coral NPU subsystem, it brings transformer and multi-stream vision acceleration to Linux-based IoT and robotics.
Because both product families build on the same architecture and compiler foundation, ML teams can optimize a model once and deploy it to a milliwatt-class wearable (Coralboard SR) or a 1 TOPS board (Coralboard SL) using the same workflow. Developed in collaboration with hardware and System-on-Module partner
Grinn
, the Coralboard lineup also gives teams a direct path from devkit prototyping to commercial production hardware.
Start building with Coral NPU
With our 32-bit architecture and v1.0 compiler stack in place, we are already working on the next phase of the roadmap, including a 64-bit Coral NPU architecture and CHERI support for security.
Whether you are designing a custom edge SoC, working on ML compilers, or deploying models to wearables and robotics, Coral NPU can help give you an open path from model to silicon. Here is where you can get started:

Summary
Mistral and NVIDIA are collaborating to revolutionize engineering workflows by integrating Mistral’s AI models with NVIDIA’s accelerated computing and physics modeling tools, enabling faster simulations and closed-loop AI-driven design. The partnership will introduce public benchmarks and open datasets to standardize evaluations for physics and agentic AI in computer-aided engineering, while leveraging NVIDIA’s Omniverse for 3D simulation and asset creation. Building on their existing work, including the development of Mistral Large 4, the initiative aims to push the boundaries of AI-powered engineering across industries like aerospace, automotive, and semiconductors.
Mistral is collaborating with NVIDIA to develop a new generation of AI-native engineering workflows powered by NVIDIA accelerated computing. Combining
Mistral Large 4
, with Mistral’s data generation, and physics modeling pipelines, accelerated by
NVIDIA CUDA-X
libraries and
NVIDIA Warp
, the initiative aims to accelerate engineering simulation and enable closed-loop workflows that connect simulation, AI model development and engineering design. Mistral and NVIDIA will also work together to integrate Mistral's models with
NVIDIA Omniverse
libraries for GPU-accelerated 3D scene generation and SimReady asset creation.
A central focus of the collaboration is the development of public benchmarks and open datasets for evaluating physics models. These benchmarks will give researchers, developers and industrial teams a shared foundation to compare model accuracy and performance and build and validate automated CAD-to-simulation workflows.
"For too long, the pace of engineering has been set by the pace of simulation. With Mistral's open-weight models and
physics AI
capabilities, combined with NVIDIA’s accelerated computing stack, we’re giving engineers faster simulation cycles, as well as open benchmarks rigorous enough to validate agents on real CAE and EDA work.” Neil Ashton, VP of Computational Engineering, Mistral
Beyond physics AI, Mistral and NVIDIA will also work together to develop dedicated evaluations and benchmarks for agentic AI in computer-aided engineering (CAE) and electronic design automation (EDA) to accelerate the application of
AI for engineering
within aerospace, automotive and semiconductor use-cases. These benchmarks will assess agents’ ability to use engineering tools, complete multistep workflows and produce technically correct results, while measuring execution time and computational cost.
Through this work, Mistral and NVIDIA will help define standards for agentic and physics AI evaluations in engineering, establishing consistent, reproducible methods for assessing capabilities and tracking progress. Powered by NVIDIA accelerated computing, libraries and tools, Mistral will redefine AI for engineering, transforming how engineers design, simulate and build the next generation of products.
“The next wave of engineering breakthroughs will come from exploring ideas that were once too complex or time-consuming to test,” said Tim Costa, vice president and general manager of industrial and computational engineering at NVIDIA. “By combining Mistral’s advanced open models and deep expertise in physics AI with NVIDIA accelerated computing and libraries, we’re helping engineers push the boundaries of design—with shared industry benchmarks to build confidence in what AI can do.”
Building on the ongoing NVIDIA and Mistral partnership
The industrial engineering collaboration builds on an ongoing partnership between NVIDIA and Mistral spanning open model development, domain-specific AI and the infrastructure needed to bring these capabilities into production.
The companies previously co-developed
Mistral NeMo
and are now
working together
through the NVIDIA Nemotron Coalition to develop a frontier base model that will continue to advance the open weight frontier. This shared foundation will enable developers and enterprises worldwide to specialize AI for their industries, languages and regions, supported by contributions of data, evaluations and domain expertise from coalition members.
Mistral recently introduced the public preview of
Mistral Large 4
, known as Le Chonk, its largest and most capable frontier model to date. With approximately 1 trillion total parameters and 49 billion active parameters, the multimodal model was trained on 3,800 NVIDIA Grace Blackwell GPUs in Mistral-operated data centers in Europe. It advances capabilities across coding, agentic workflows and multimodal understanding, with weights planned for release at the end of October.
Alongside model development, Mistral and NVIDIA are expanding the infrastructure that powers AI training, customization and inference. Mistral is bringing additional NVIDIA-powered AI infrastructure online in support of Mistral’s compute roadmap targeting 1 GW of capacity by 2030.
This expansion strengthens Europe’s role in developing and delivering AI for the world. By connecting European infrastructure and research with open models, specialized engineering capabilities and customer applications, Mistral and NVIDIA are helping enterprises build AI around their own expertise and scale it to serve markets worldwide.

Voxtral 3 introduces a cutting-edge voice agent SDK and state-of-the-art speech models designed for real-time, multi-step conversations across 50+ languages. It combines accurate transcription, natural speech synthesis with emotional adaptability, and deep tool integration for seamless workflow automation. Available via Mistral’s EU-hosted API or self-deployment, it ensures data sovereignty while delivering low-latency, human-like interactions for contact centers, virtual assistants, and hands-free copilots.
Speech transcription and voice generation have come a long way, but building end-to-end voice agents that can listen, reason, interact, and handle complex workflows remains difficult.
A reliable voice agent needs to do four things very well (and simultaneously):
Listen accurately
across languages, accents, speakers, and interruptions,
Reason

Speak naturally

Take action

Getting all four to work together reliably in real time remains a challenge.

and

models, alongside a voice agent SDK that brings listening, thinking, tool calling, and speaking into a single real-time streaming pipeline.
Voxtral 3 is built to create natural conversational experiences, from contact-center agents and service desks to virtual assistants and hands-free copilots. As with other Mistral models, the Voxtral 3 family is designed for sovereign deployment. . The speech-to-text model,

Pro Voice for distinctly accurate voice adaptation
. For professional use cases where basic voice cloning does not suffice, Voxtral’s

Your voice AI, on your infrastructure

It hears 50+ languages, with state-of-the-art accuracy.
Voxtral Transcribe 3

A good teacher meets the student where they are
A new self-distillation method that jointly trains teacher and student to improve model performance and training efficiency on complex reasoning and agentic tasks.

Authors
Perplexity Research & NVIDIA
Introduction
Reinforcement Learning (RL) is widely used in post-training language models to improve their capabilities on complex reasoning and long-horizon agentic tasks.
In a typical setup, the model makes repeated attempts at a task, receives an outcome reward for each, and learns to favor actions taken in higher-reward attempts. However, a single outcome reward provides a sparse learning signal that does not distinguish which intermediate actions helped or hurt the outcome. This sparsity limits sample efficiency, especially on difficult agentic tasks, where attempts are long and successes are rare.
One popular approach to addressing this sparsity is On-Policy Distillation (OPD), which uses a stronger teacher model to give token by token guidance to the studentâs own attempts, providing much denser rewards. However, teaching is a skill in itself. A model that is good at solving a task is not necessarily good at teaching it, as its feedback may be beyond the studentâs current capabilities. This motivates training not only the student to imitate the teacher but also the teacher to provide better-aligned guidance to the student.
We propose one such method,
Joint On-policy Learning and Teaching
(JOLT). Building on On-Policy Self-Distillation (OPSD), we use a single model in two roles: a teacher with access to privileged information, such as verified solutions, and a student without such access. We train the two roles jointly. The student follows the standard distillation objective. The teacherâs objective pushes its feedback to move the student in the same direction as RL on the student's own reward. Together, these objectives train the teacher to meet the student where they are and help the student learn from guidance within their reach.
Our experiments demonstrate improvements in both model performance and training efficiency across a range of mathematical reasoning, coding, and agentic tasks.
